evidence.title: Model Predictive Coolant Allocation for Integrated Tab-Surface Cooling of Battery Cells
evidence.abstract: Battery electrical tab cooling is effective at reducing internal thermal gradients by exploiting the high thermal conductivity of the current collectors, whereas surface cooling is effective at reducing temperature rise because of its large heat transfer area. Using either strategy alone, however, limits the achievable trade-off between thermal uniformity and temperature rise reduction. This work proposes an integrated tab-surface cooling (ITSC) system in which coolant is dynamically allocated among the lateral surface and tab channels. The allocation is formulated as an optimal control problem in which the battery temperature is regulated towards a desired reference and thermal gradients are minimised. To support this formulation, a first-principles coolant model is developed and coupled with battery and valve-actuation models. The resulting optimal coolant-allocation problem is solved using a computationally efficient real-time iteration model predictive control (RTI-MPC) scheme, with a nonlinear MPC serving as a closed-loop performance benchmark. Evaluation results under realistic driving conditions showed that RTI-MPC reproduces the nonlinear MPC thermal response with absolute errors below 0.0035 degC while reducing the computational cost from several seconds to 19.3 ms, indicating strong potential for real-time implementation. Additionally, evaluation of the proposed ITSC system against conventional cooling configurations demonstrates that ITSC achieves the best overall trade-off between temperature regulation and thermal gradient reduction.

evidence.title: Particle cooling in Vaporizing Coolant
evidence.abstract: The approximate mathematical model for a cooling of the particle in a volatile liquid is developed and analyzed. Despite the precise model is complex and requires the solution of the nonstationary two-phase flow equations with the conjugated heat transfer boundary problem for the particle, vapor, and liquid cooling pool, the considered simple model may be of interest. Vapor is permanently produced and removed from the coolant pool. Analysis of the model obtained resulted in some correlations for the three main parameters of the cooling process, which may be used for estimation of the particle cooling.

evidence.title: Limits of sympathetic cooling of fermions: The role of the heat capacity of the coolant
evidence.abstract: The sympathetic cooling of an initially degenerate Fermi gas by either an ideal Bose gas below $T_c$ or an ideal Boltzmann gas is investigated. It is shown that the efficiency of cooling by a Bose gas below $T_c$ is by no means reduced when its heat capacity becomes much less than that of the Fermi gas, where efficiency is measured by the decrease in the temperature of the Fermi gas per number of particles evaporated from the coolant. This contradicts the intuitive idea that an efficient coolant must have a large heat capacity. In contrast, for a Boltzmann gas a minimal value of the ratio of the heat capacities is indeed necessary to achieve T=0 and all of the particles must be evaporated.

mechanism_map.mechanism: Dynamic, model-directed allocation of coolant among parallel branches: a first-principles coolant model coupled with valve-actuation models predicts each branch's thermal/flow response, so commanded allocation can be compared against measured response to localize a flow-path anomaly.
mechanism_map.intervention: Add (or reuse) shut-off/bypass valves to sequentially command coolant flow to individual engine-cooling branches—driver-side heater core, radiator, engine block, heater bypass—while logging branch inlet/outlet temperature, flow, and system pressure, and compare each transient against a first-principles model of the circuit, mirroring the paper's closed-loop comparison of predicted vs. actual thermal response.
mechanism_map.expected_effect: The seeping branch shows a model-prediction mismatch (missing flow, lagging temperature rise, or pressure decay) with no visible drip, localizing the leak—most plausibly the driver-side heater core or its connections, matching the stronger driver-side coolant smell.
mechanism_map.falsification_test: Warm and pressurize the system, command flow only to the heater-core branch, and hold; if the model's predicted outlet-temperature rise and pressure hold are not met (outlet lags, pressure decays), the leak is in that branch—confirm by dye/borescope after isolation; if every branch matches model predictions within tolerance, the mechanism is falsified and the source is external seepage evaporating on a hot surface.
mechanism_map.mechanism_source_span: coolant is dynamically allocated among the lateral surface and tab channels

candidates.mechanism: Coolant seepage through gasket/seal interfaces is driven by thermal-gradient-induced differential expansion and pressure transients; seepate evaporates on hot metal before it can pool, so no drip is visible — only odor and residue. Dynamically allocating coolant among parallel engine cooling circuits (block lateral surface vs. cylinder-head/tab-adjacent channels) regulates metal temperature toward a reference while minimizing spatial thermal gradients, which reduces cyclic differential expansion and pressure spikes at sealing interfaces and therefore the seepage driving force.
candidates.intervention: Add an integrated tab-surface-style cooling allocation layer to the engine cooling system: independently actuated valves on the block/lateral-surface circuit and the cylinder-head/tab circuit, governed by a first-principles coolant model coupled to engine-thermal and valve-actuation models and solved with a real-time iteration model predictive control (RTI-MPC) scheme that commands the coolant split to track a temperature reference while minimizing head-to-block thermal gradients.

evidence_bundle.mechanism_source_span: an integrated tab-surface cooling (ITSC) system in which coolant is dynamically allocated among the lateral surface and tab channels. The allocation is formulated as an optimal control problem in which the battery temperature is regulated towards a desired reference and thermal gradients are minimised.

constraint_set.problem_constraint: must locate leak source despite no visible drip during dealership inspection
constraint_set.boundary_conditions: Engine running with a functional water pump, coolant above freezing and within specified concentration, actuators responsive within the real-time control horizon, and heat rejection within radiator and heater-core capacity.

candidates.predicted_effect: Lower spatial thermal gradient across the head/block interface and lower pressure transients, producing a measurable drop in coolant consumption rate (mass loss per distance), less dried-residue accumulation near the driver-side head-gasket region, and reduced post-drive coolant odor intensity, with the closed-loop thermal response matching a nonlinear-MPC benchmark to within ~0.0035 degC at ~19.3 ms solve cost.
known_failure_modes: valve actuator stiction or freezing locks the split and reintroduces gradients
coolant-model drift causes the controller to command maldistribution
temperature/pressure sensor loss degrades gradient minimization
loss of compute forces fixed-flow fallback
fouling or blockage in the narrow tab channel causes localized overheating and renewed seepage
candidates.novel_design_variable: The MPC-commanded coolant allocation fraction between the block (lateral-surface) channel and the cylinder-head (tab) channel as a function of load and temperature — i.e., the dynamic valve split ratio.
candidates.testable_prediction: On an identical driving cycle, the RTI-MPC allocated engine will show a statistically significant reduction in measured head-to-block temperature gradient and in coolant loss per 1000 km versus fixed-flow cooling, with residue mass near the driver-side head gasket reduced; the hypothesis is falsified if neither the gradient nor the coolant-loss rate differs significantly between configurations.

custody_records.raw_content: Battery electrical tab cooling is effective at reducing internal thermal gradients by exploiting the high thermal conductivity of the current collectors, whereas surface cooling is effective at reducing temperature rise because of its large heat transfer area. Using either strategy alone, however, limits the achievable trade-off between thermal uniformity and temperature rise reduction. This work proposes an integrated tab-surface cooling (ITSC) system in which coolant is dynamically allocated among the lateral surface and tab channels. The allocation is formulated as an optimal control problem in which the battery temperature is regulated towards a desired reference and thermal gradients are minimised. To support this formulation, a first-principles coolant model is developed and coupled with battery and valve-actuation models. The resulting optimal coolant-allocation problem is solved using a computationally efficient real-time iteration model predictive control (RTI-MPC) scheme, with a nonlinear MPC serving as a closed-loop performance benchmark. Evaluation results under realistic driving conditions showed that RTI-MPC reproduces the nonlinear MPC thermal response with absolute errors below 0.0035 degC while reducing the computational cost from several seconds to 19.3 ms, indicating strong potential for real-time implementation. Additionally, evaluation of the proposed ITSC system against conventional cooling configurations demonstrates that ITSC achieves the best overall trade-off between temperature regulation and thermal gradient reduction.

custody_records.raw_content: The approximate mathematical model for a cooling of the particle in a volatile liquid is developed and analyzed. Despite the precise model is complex and requires the solution of the nonstationary two-phase flow equations with the conjugated heat transfer boundary problem for the particle, vapor, and liquid cooling pool, the considered simple model may be of interest. Vapor is permanently produced and removed from the coolant pool. Analysis of the model obtained resulted in some correlations for the three main parameters of the cooling process, which may be used for estimation of the particle cooling.

custody_records.raw_content: The sympathetic cooling of an initially degenerate Fermi gas by either an ideal Bose gas below $T_c$ or an ideal Boltzmann gas is investigated. It is shown that the efficiency of cooling by a Bose gas below $T_c$ is by no means reduced when its heat capacity becomes much less than that of the Fermi gas, where efficiency is measured by the decrease in the temperature of the Fermi gas per number of particles evaporated from the coolant. This contradicts the intuitive idea that an efficient coolant must have a large heat capacity. In contrast, for a Boltzmann gas a minimal value of the ratio of the heat capacities is indeed necessary to achieve T=0 and all of the particles must be evaporated.
